data.content_ref: inline:The target's own criterion is internally self-defeating: it claims we should prefer theories that have 'minimized known error relative to alternatives,' but 'known error' is only detectable through testing. A theory that has never been subjected to any test has zero known errors—the absolute minimum. On the target's stated logic, an untested, contentless, or unfalsifiable claim (zero detected errors) is strictly preferable to a bold, heavily tested theory that has accumulated even one known error. This is distinct from the prior objections (which attacked the Popper analogy and the induction smuggle); it shows the criterion collapses on its own terms, independent of whether it faithfully represents Popper or avoids induction. The 'deficit of truth' subtraction model provides no mechanism to distinguish 'no errors because untested' from 'no errors because severely tested and survived,' making 'minimized known error' a vacuous and counterproductive preference rule.
